lessons.title: Where the stress falls
lessons.goal: Find the stressed syllable of any word from its spelling, and hear when stress changes the meaning.

tip.title: Two rules and a tilde
tip.body: Spanish stress is predictable from spelling. Words ending in a vowel, n or s stress the second-to-last syllable: casa, hablan, martes. Words ending in any other consonant stress the last syllable: hablar, ciudad, español. When a word breaks these rules, a written accent (tilde) marks the stressed vowel: café, canción, árbol, música. Stress can change meaning: término (end, term), termino (I finish), terminó (he/she finished); hablo (I speak), habló (he/she spoke). Make the stressed syllable a little longer and higher, but keep every unstressed vowel full and clear: don't reduce them to the "uh" of English "banana". Papá is "pa-PÁ", not "PUH-pa".

phrases.note: Papa is potato in Latin America and the Canary Islands; in mainland Spain it's patata. El papa is the Pope.
Animo, without the tilde, means "I encourage".

stress.note: Papá breaks the vowel rule, so it needs a tilde; papas follows it.
Público stresses the third-to-last syllable: words like this always carry a tilde.

stress.t: Hoy canto yo; ayer cantó ella.
stress.n: Today I sing; yesterday she sang.
stress.note: Canto (I sing) vs cantó (she sang): only the stress tells them apart.

stress.t: Termino el trabajo a las cinco.

lessons.title: Tú or tu? Qué or que?
lessons.goal: Stress tú, él, mí, sí, más and question words; keep tu, el, mi, si and que light.

tip.title: The tilde shows the stressed twin
tip.body: Some short words come in pairs: one is stressed and carries a tilde, the other is unstressed and leans on the next word. Tú (you), él (he), mí (me), sí (yes), más (more), té (tea) are stressed; tu (your), el (the), mi (my), si (if), mas (but, only in literary writing), te (you, object) are not. Say "tu casa" as one word, "tucasa", but give tú its own beat: "¿Y tú?". Question words are stressed too: qué, cómo, cuándo, dónde, quién, also inside a sentence ("No sé qué quiere"). Que, como, cuando and donde without a tilde are linking words and stay light. In English you might stress "if" or "that" for emphasis; in Spanish, keep si and que unstressed.

phrases.n: How is he? Same as always.
Do you want more? No, thanks.
I don't know what she wants.

stress.note: Tú gets a beat; tu runs into libro.

stress.n: How is he? Same as always.
stress.note: Cómo asks a question and is stressed; como (as, like) is light.
